title: Ten Years of Reinforcement Learning (2016–2026)
content: Between 2016 and 2026, reinforcement learning (RL) expanded from perfect-information board games to large-scale simulation, offline control, language-model post-training, and interactive reasoning agents. Across these settings, much of the algorithmic terminology persisted, including Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS), value estimation, clipped policy ratios, offline conservatism, and self-play. Yet the operating assumptions underneath those methods changed completely with respect to simulator fidelity, logged-data coverage, evaluator reliability, and prior competence. Consequently, classical deep-RL research and modern foundation-model post-training often talk past one another, treating surface similarities as inherited algorithms or misdiagnosing why familiar optimizers stall under new environment constraints. This article examines that decade-long technical progression by placing four overlapping regimes, namely self-play and deep RL foundations (2016–2018), large-scale RL, world models, and offline RL (2018–2022), preference post-training (2020–2023), and verifiable-reward RL for reasoning and interactive agents (2023–2026), into a common notation to compare their actual optimization objectives, data access, and failure boundaries. We distinguish documented methodological inheritance from cross-era functional analogies (such as tree search versus test-time compute, learned value functions versus reward models or verifiers, offline support constraints versus preference shift, and symmetric self-play versus verifiable rollouts) and identify the specific operating assumption that breaks on transfer. Extending the same comparison to robotics, traffic control, chip floorplanning, clinical care, and theorem proving reveals a consistent pattern: whether RL succeeds or yields to imitation, supervised learning, or symbolic verification depends primarily on having a cheap and faithful evaluator, queryable transitions, and an adequate prior, more than on the choice of optimizer. Seen in this light, the main open problems of 2026, including verifier generality, long-horizon entropy collapse, proxy overoptimization, and the boundary between capability elicitation and new learning, are direct continuations of bottlenecks that have recurred throughout the decade.
